rationale: A wins because it keeps the story tied to the supplied facts: "Duolingo's beta language video chats are holding users for 9 minutes a session" is a usable engagement-data angle with the right caveats. B has sharper teeth in places, especially "A profitable public company is giving away chess and charging for the AI," but it opens by saying users are talking to Duolingo's "cartoon owl" when the update says Lily. That is how a decent strategy memo turns into an apology email.
gaps_in_A: "The video feature is in beta now" overstates the timing; the update says beta engagement averaged 9 minutes, not that the feature remains in beta at announcement time.
"Educators are skeptical, Duolingo is doubling down" uses a blacklisted cliche and makes the company posture sound more adversarial than the facts prove.
"spoken video chat, a gamified chess course" slightly smears the gamification critique across chess; the update says chess is launching free, not that the chess course itself is gamified.
The chess angle is viable but still needs a harder executive rationale; "why Duolingo chose chess specifically" is not a detail, it is the hinge of the story.
gaps_in_B: "talking to its cartoon owl" invents the protagonist. The update says users talk to Lily, not the owl.
"most-criticized design" overclaims. The facts say some educators criticized gamification as shallow learning, not that this is Duolingo's central or most criticized design issue.
"live, unscripted spoken conversation" adds "unscripted" without support from the update.
"existing music or math courses" drags in outside product context. The caveat helps, but in a blind source-limited angle set it still muddies the grounding.
